blocks.text: Most animators who use Photoshop do frame-by-frame work. You draw one frame, step to the next, and draw again until the motion reads. The frames live in the Timeline panel. Photoshop also handles the work around the motion: cleanup of rough sketches, color and texture passes, and layouts for a shot. This page covers that workflow, the snags people report, and where Lazur fits in.
Where Photoshop fits in animation work on Mac

Photoshop rarely does a whole motion job alone. In a 2021 School of Motion survey of about 2,100 artists, animators and designers, 78.2% of motion designers named After Effects as their most-used software. Nearly 17% also work in Cinema 4D. These figures reach us through Mark Studios, which compiles them. Check the original before you quote them.

Photoshop turns up in hiring more often than you might expect. Across 2025 US job postings for special effects artists and animators, 49% mention Adobe Photoshop. Illustrator appears in 43%. After Effects appears in 32%. The sample size is not stated, and the figures measure what employers ask for, not what freelancers use each day. Treat them as a hiring signal, not a usage survey.

So the practical split is simple. Use Photoshop for drawing, cleanup and reference work. Use After Effects, or another motion tool, for timing that has to run across many layers. Ask the people you work with which files they expect from you, because pipelines differ from studio to studio.

Before you open a file, decide which job it is. A rough pose sheet, a cleanup pass on a scanned drawing and a background color test all belong in Photoshop. A shot that needs eased motion across many properties usually belongs somewhere else. That decision saves more time than any shortcut. It also tells you which file format to hand over at the end.
Set up frame-by-frame animation in Photoshop

Open the Timeline from Window > Timeline. Photoshop's Timeline panel can offer a frame animation view or a video timeline. Animators usually want the frame view for drawing. Check which view the panel shows before you draw anything. Menu names can change between builds, so read the panel menu on your version.

items: Set the canvas size first. Changing it after drawing can crop your art.
Make one layer per moving part, such as a body, an arm or a prop. Name each one.
Duplicate the last frame to trace over it, then lower the drawing's opacity so you can see the earlier pose.
Play the sequence from the Timeline before you clean up timing. Find problems while they are still cheap to fix.
Save a PSD backup to a separate folder before any import or export.

blocks.text: Choose a canvas size that matches the final output. Some animators draw larger than the delivery size and scale down. Test that approach on a short shot first. If the edges look soft after scaling, change the approach before you draw the whole sequence.

Here is a short bounce as a worked example. Draw the ground on a locked layer, so you never draw on it by accident. Then draw the ball at rest on its own layer. Next draw the squash, where the ball flattens on impact. Draw the stretch as it leaves the ground. Play those drawings back before you add the in-between frames. If the squash looks like a pancake, shrink it and draw it again.
Photoshop timeline animation: draw each frame without losing your place

The clearest first-hand report on this comes from an animator with about ten years of Photoshop animation work. Their post, dated February 24, 2026, says they must click each frame manually before drawing on it. They want to move to the next frame and draw straight away. The post had 57 views and 2 replies, so it is one voice, not a survey. It is still a useful checklist of what frustrates working animators.

Until the workflow gets smoother, build a habit that keeps you on track. Select the frame, read its number in the panel, then draw. Do this every time, even for a quick pose. Skipping that step is how drawings land on the wrong frame, and you find out during playback.

A quick check helps here. After you draw a frame, read the frame number before you move on. Then play a few frames forward and back. If a pose jumps, the drawing went on the wrong frame. Moving it takes seconds now and much longer after the whole sequence is drawn.
Cut tool, bucket fill and gaps in animation drawings

The same February 2026 post says the Cut tool feels unintuitive. It also says the bucket fill struggles when an area is not fully closed. The author compares it with other drawing software that handles those cases better. Treat both points as a warning, not a verdict. Your line work decides most of how a fill behaves.

rows: Bucket fill leaks through a gap
Close the gap on its own layer with a brush, then fill on a layer under the line art.
Bucket fill ignores part of the shape
Check the bucket's sample option. Changing it to all layers can change what the fill reads.
Cutting a drawing into parts feels awkward
Select the area with a lasso, then press ⌘J to copy it to a new layer.
Line art and color bleed together
Keep line art on one layer and color on another, so each can change alone.
blocks.caption: Common gap and fill problems, with a first thing to try. Test each fix on a short shot.

blocks.text: Usually a gap is a drawing problem, not a tool problem. Zoom in and look for the tiny break first. Small gaps often hide at the corners of a pose. Fix the line on a separate layer, then fill again. You save time by fixing the drawing instead of fighting the bucket.

Watch for gaps that show on one frame only. Compare that frame with the frames before and after it. If the break appears only where a line crosses a shadow, the problem is that line. Copy the good frame, redraw the line on its own layer, and paste the fix back in.
Import video reference without freezing Photoshop

A February 2026 Adobe Community post reports that dragging a .mov file into the Photoshop timeline can turn the screen black. It says the app then freezes or crashes. The same author reports frequent crashes in general. One report does not prove a bug on your Mac. It is still a good reason to save first and keep your reference separate.

items: Save your PSD and close other heavy apps before you import anything.
Keep the reference video open in QuickTime Player beside Photoshop, and step through it by eye.
If you need frames from video, export a still image sequence from your video app, then bring the stills in.
Keep the original video in its own folder. A crash should cost you minutes, not the reference.

blocks.text: Image sequences take longer to set up. They also give you one file per frame, which is easier to fix when a single pose is wrong. That trade is usually worth it for a shot you plan to revisit.
Layers, names and cleanup for animation files

Name layers the way you would name shots. A short code that gives the character, the action and the pose works well. Something like hero_walk_contact stays easy to search after a week of drawing. Vague names like Layer 4 slow you down every time you open the file.

Here is a worked example. You animate a door opening. Put the door frame on a locked layer, the door on its own layer, and the shadow on a third layer. Each frame then changes only the door and the shadow. If the shadow needs a new shape, you edit that one layer, and the frame and door stay as they are.

Cleanup goes faster when each layer has one job. Keep rough sketches on a layer with lower opacity, and hide that layer before you ink. Draw the clean line on a new layer. Delete the rough layer only after the shot is approved, not before.
Mistakes that slow animators down

items: Drawing on the background layer, so a cleanup pass erases part of the scene.
Merging layers early, which removes your ability to fix one element on its own.
Skipping a save before a long import or export.
Saving versions as final, final2 and final_real in one folder.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes cost time later, not now. A merged layer looks fine until someone asks for one arm to move. Save a copy before each big change, and write a short note on what changed. That habit takes a minute and saves an afternoon.
Keyboard shortcuts for drawing and cleanup on Mac

These shortcuts are Photoshop defaults on macOS. They cover most drawing and cleanup tasks. If one does nothing, someone may have remapped it. Check Edit > Keyboard Shortcuts to see the current setup.

items: ⌘Z undoes the last step.
⌘J copies the current selection to a new layer.
⌘⇧N creates a new layer.
[ and ] make the brush smaller and larger.
B selects the Brush tool. E selects the Eraser.

blocks.text: Shortcuts help most when your hand is already on the tablet. Learn the five or six you use most before you chase the rest. Print them and tape them near the tablet if that helps you.
Check playback before you export frames

Play the loop at full size, then again at the size it will be delivered. A pose can read well on a large canvas and blur when it shrinks. Look for jitter at the edges of the frame, where small shifts show most. Mark each frame that feels wrong with a note in its layer name, so you can find it later.

Export a PNG sequence into a new folder, never over an old export. Name the folder with the shot and the date. Open the sequence in a second app to confirm the order. A wrong order is easy to miss in Photoshop and obvious in playback.
What Photoshop costs for animators in 2026

Adobe's product page lists standalone Photoshop at US$22.99 per month, billed monthly on an annual commitment. A prepaid annual plan is US$263.88 per year. Creative Cloud Pro is listed at US$69.99 per month after an intro offer. Prices can vary by region and promotion, so check Adobe's pricing page before you buy.

blocks.text: The Photoshop product page does not mention a timeline, frame animation or video editing inside Photoshop. Its closest item is Rotate Object, which tilts, rotates and scales objects in real time. So treat Photoshop as a drawing and cleanup tool for animation, not an animation suite. Compare its cost with the apps you open every week.

Count the cost of lost work too. If a crash eats an afternoon, the monthly price matters less than your schedule. Save often, keep backups, and choose a plan you can keep paying for through a full project.
Photoshop 27.11 and the timeline

CG Channel dates its Photoshop 27.11 article to Tuesday, October 6, 2026. Its listed features include Enhance Edge for Remove Background masks, GPT Image 2 for Generate Image and Prompt to edit, and renaming and deletion of Recents in New Document. The article does not mention timeline, animation or video changes. Don't count on an update to fix a frame workflow problem. Read Adobe's release notes for your build first.

If you want to test a new build, duplicate your project file first. Run the test on a short shot. Check the Timeline, your brush settings and your import steps before you open a long job in the new version.
How Lazur helps while you animate in Photoshop

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘, which is Option plus Command, to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate Photoshop for you. You keep the pen, the tablet and every decision about the drawing. That limit suits frame work, where the timing is yours. Lazur helps most when you lose the panel, forget a menu path or want a term explained.

Ask short questions. What does this icon do? gets a spoken answer based on what is on screen. Where is the Timeline panel? gets a circle and a label. Lazur cannot see your shot idea, so describe the problem in plain words, such as the pose that jumps.

Dictation runs in any app. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor. Use it for shot notes, file names and messages to a director, then fix the wording by hand. Dictation is unlimited, so it does not use up your AI actions.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. If your project is under an NDA, check that rule against your studio's policy before you use voice help on that screen.
Next steps for your first animation week

items: Open Window > Timeline and draw one short bounce, with one layer per moving part.
Save a PSD, then export a PNG sequence to a separate folder.
Play the loop and mark the frames that feel wrong.
Ask Lazur where a control is whenever you lose your place.

faq.question: Can you animate in Photoshop on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Photoshop has a Timeline panel for frame-by-frame work, and you can open it from Window > Timeline. Many animators use it for drawing and cleanup. Motion graphics usually happen in After Effects, so plan your saves and file structure around that split.

faq.question: Is Photoshop the right tool for motion graphics?
faq.answer: Usually not on its own. In a 2021 School of Motion survey, 78.2% of motion designers named After Effects as their most-used software, according to Mark Studios. Photoshop fits drawing and cleanup better than timing across many layers.

faq.question: Why does Photoshop freeze when I import a .mov file?
faq.answer: One animator reported in February 2026 that dragging a .mov file into the timeline froze or crashed Photoshop. That is one post, not proof of a fault on your Mac. Import image sequences instead, and save before you import.

faq.question: Does Photoshop 27.11 fix timeline problems?
faq.answer: CG Channel's article on Photoshop 27.11, dated October 6, 2026, does not mention timeline, animation or video changes. Read Adobe's release notes for your build before you assume a fix.

faq.question: How much does Photoshop cost for animators?
faq.answer: Adobe lists standalone Photoshop at US$22.99 per month, billed monthly on an annual commitment, or US$263.88 per year prepaid. Prices vary by region and promotion. Check Adobe's pricing page before you buy.

faq.question: What can Lazur do inside Photoshop?
faq.answer: Lazur answers out loud, points at things and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate Photoshop for you. You stay in control of the drawing.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
